steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer

1. Goal  
   Turn one sequence of symbols (words, DNA bases, pixels, etc.) into another sequence or into a single prediction, while remembering long-range relationships, all in parallel.

2. Key idea: Attention instead of recurrence  
   Earlier sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs) processed tokens one-by-one; they implicitly stored history in hidden states.  
   Transformers let every token look directly at every other token through “attention”—a learned weighting of how much each token should care about the rest. Because attention can be computed for all tokens at once, the model trains faster and can capture arbitrarily long dependencies.

3. Inside one Transformer layer
   a. Input embeddings  
      Each token is converted to a vector. Positional information (sine/cosine or learned vectors) is added so the model knows order.

   b. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
      For every token i produce three vectors by linear projection:
        • Query   Qᵢ (“What am I looking for?”)  
        • Key     Kᵢ (“What characteristics do I have?”)  
        • Value   Vᵢ (“Information to pass along”)  

      Attention weight between token i and j = softmax(Qᵢ·Kⱼ / √d).  
      Output for i = Σⱼ attention_weightᵢⱼ · Vⱼ.  

      “Multi-head” means we repeat this with different learned projections, letting the model focus on different relations (e.g., subject–verb, coreference).

   c. Add & Norm  
      Add the attention output back to the original input (residual connection), then layer-normalize to stabilize training.

   d. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
      A small two-layer MLP applies to each position separately:  
      FF(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁)W₂ + b₂.  
      Another Add & Norm follows.

4. Stacking  
   A Transformer is just many identical layers (e.g., 6, 12, 48). Depth lets the model refine representations.

5. Encoder vs. Decoder  
   Encoder (BERT, ViT): processes an input sequence and returns contextual embeddings.  
   Decoder (GPT): like encoder but with causal (look-left-only) attention so each token can’t see future tokens, enabling autoregressive generation.  
   Seq2Seq (original Vaswani et al.): encoder produces memory; decoder attends to that memory plus its own left-context to emit output tokens.

6. Training objectives  
   • Language modelling: predict next token (GPT).  
   • Masked token prediction (BERT).  
   • Paired source-target prediction (translation, summarization).  
   Loss is usually cross-entropy between predicted distribution and true tokens.

7. Learning and inference  
   During training, back-propagation adjusts all linear projection and FF weights so that attention patterns and transformations minimize loss.  
   During inference, attention weights become dynamic, letting the model flexibly route information for each new input.

8. Why it works  
   • Attention is content-based, so distance in the original sequence doesn’t matter.  
   • Parallelism: GPUs evaluate all positions simultaneously.  
   • Residual + normalization ease gradient flow.  
   • Multi-head attention allows disentangling multiple relationships.

9. Limitations & advances  
   Quadratic cost in sequence length → research into sparse, linear, and long-range variants (Performer, Longformer).  
   Size scales well with data: bigger models keep improving (scaling laws).  
   Extensions: vision (ViT), audio, multimodal, retrieval-augmented, etc.

In short, a Transformer turns “Which other tokens matter to me?” into a differentiable, globally parallel lookup table. By iteratively re-weighing tokens and mixing information through feed-forward blocks, it builds rich representations that power modern NLP and beyond.
